newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China ferro-silicon export expansion seen hampered.
newsitem.headline: China ferro-silicon export expansion seen hampered.

text.p: China's 1997 ferro-silicon export licences have been issued but exporters are concerned over continued European anti-dumping tariffs and obstacles in developing other markets, a Chinese trader said on Tuesday.
"China has issued this year's export licences for ferro-silicon," said the trader who declined to be identified.
He did not specify how many licences were issued, but told Reuters that every year China authorised between 400,000 to 500,000 tonnes of ferro-silicon exports.
China would try this year to appeal for a review of Europe's 45 percent anti-dumping tariff on Chinese ferro-silicon, the source said.
"In effect, the tariff means that European markets are closed to Chinese ferro-silicon," the source noted, adding that the tariff was largely aimed at protecting Norwegian ferro-silicon producers.
The trader was participating in a week-long fair in Hong Kong sponsored by the China Iron and Steel Industry and Trade Group Corp (CSGC) and China Metallurgic (Hong Kong) Company Ltd.
While ferro-silicon in Europe cost about US$900-1,000 a tonne, CIF Rotterdam, Chinese ferro-silicon is priced at an average of $750 a tonne, FOB China.
"With about $80 per tonne in freight charges, Chinese ferro-silicon still costs about $830 per tonne, CIF Rotterdam," the trader said.
China's cheap labour and lax environmental laws made ferro-silicon relatively cheap to produce, the source said, noting that China lost out to Brazil as far as the European market was concerned.
"Brazilian ferro-silicon is cheaper than Europe's, but more expensive than China's," he said.
China's ferro-silicon industry relied heavily on demand from Japan's steel industry and East Asian markets such as Taiwan and the Philippines.
"We would like to develop markets in India and sub-Saharan Africa, where demand is very strong, but the risk is too high," the trader said.
Indian firms' capacity to pay was inconsistent, and buyers wanted letters of credit for 180 days, which was not acceptable to Chinese traders, the source said, also pointing to high port charges.

"The risk in India, and the political instability risk in Africa makes doing business difficult," he said. Ferro-silicon is one of the main ferro-alloys added to iron to make steel and China is the biggest producer of ferro-silicon in the world, the trader said.
Every tonne of steel contains about one to three percent ferro-alloy.
China itself consumes about one million tonnes of ferro-silicon a year, the source said.
